Text: The lab sides a loose bone in three steps: name the bone, find its {{c1::anterior and posterior}} faces, then use one medial or lateral landmark to call left or right.
Back Extra:
Why: many bones look right either way until you know which face is the front and which end is up; after that, one medial or lateral landmark settles the side.

Cue: on the practical the bone lies loose in any orientation, so pick it up and turn it into anatomical position first.

Text: The lab names every bone's orientation as if the body were in {{c1::anatomical position}}.
Back Extra:
Why: anatomical position is standing upright with the palms facing forward, so the thumbs point outward and the radius and its styloid process count as lateral even when your own forearm is turned.

Pitfall: a relaxed arm hangs palm-in, which makes the radius look anterior; always name sides as if the palms faced forward.

Text: A {{c1::fossa}} is a {{c2::shallow depression}} in a bone where another structure sits.
Back Extra: Why: a fossa gives a neighboring part room to sit, like the olecranon fossa on the back of the humerus, which takes the ulna's olecranon when you straighten your elbow.

Text: A {{c1::foramen}} is a {{c2::hole::kind of bone marking}} in a bone that nerves and blood vessels pass through.
Back Extra:
Why: nerves and vessels have to cross bone to reach what they supply, so bones have holes where they pass; the obturator foramen of the hip bone is the largest in the body.

Pitfall: as a bone marking, a foramen is a hole through bone; the instructor said openings in muscles are not called foramina.

Text: About {{c1::99::percent}}% of the body's calcium is stored in the bones.
Back Extra: Why: bone mineral is calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite), so the skeleton doubles as the body's calcium bank and releases calcium into the blood when levels drop.

Text: The fetal skull bones are not fused; they are joined by areas of connective tissue called {{c1::fontanels}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the bones ossify from separate centers and don't meet and fuse until after birth.

Cue: the fontanels are the baby's 'soft spots' and last for months after birth.
